newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt to free Shi'ite detainees.
newsitem.headline: Egypt to free Shi'ite detainees.

text.p: Egypt has decided to set free a group of people who were accused of promoting ideas of the Islamic branch of Shi'ism in the Arab country, a public prosecution official said on Wednesday.
Hisham Saraya told reporters he had granted release from detention for a group which included 56 people detained since September and nine held last month.
A lawyer for one of the detained, Mukhtar Nuah, had told Reuters on Monday that the 56 would be freed.
They were held pending security investigations but they were never formally charged in court.

In the same language it uses for Moslem militants, the interior ministry had said it wanted to question the detainees on suspicion of "subverting the constitution, preventing authorities from enforcing it, harming national unity and social order, and exploiting religion."
The Egyptian newspaper al-Gomhouria on Monday said one of them, preacher Sheikh Hassan Shehata, was accused of spreading Shi'ite ideas including temporary marriage.
Shi'ism is a branch of Egypt's official religion Islam and the dominant sect in Iran. It is not illegal in Egypt but the government is wary of any Iranian religious influence.
The detention of the group highlighted the often tense ties between Egypt and Shi'ite Iran, which Cairo often accuses of supporting militant groups trying to impose a strict Islamic state in Egypt.
This month Interior Minister Hassan el-Alfi accused Iran of continuing to support the militant Gama'a al-Islamiya, the largest organisation fighting to overthrow Egypt's government.
Iran denies the accusations. It says Egypt tries to cover up internal problems rooted in Cairo's pro-Western policies.
Shi'ites and Sunnis differ originally over who should have led the Moslem community on Prophet Mohammad's death. Differences in doctrine, law and politics developed.
